content.chapter: Chapter 1: A Hospital Ahead of Its Time
objectives: Explain why the complex is described as ahead of its time.
Compare the dates in Anatolia and Europe precisely.
Identify the role of Konya and Kayseri at the time.
Use reduced relative clauses, not … until, while and be regarded as.
content.pedagogy: The opening chapter makes a strong historical claim and supports it with a chain of comparisons. Dense noun phrases with reduced relative clauses (“training established in Anatolia”, “School … established by Sultan Mahmud II”) are typical of academic English and are the main reading challenge.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The complex was built in honor of Gevher Nesibe, not by her.
“More than 600 years after” refers to the Imperial Medical School, not to the complex itself.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: reduced relative clauses (established by …) · not … until / It was not until … that · while (contrast) · be regarded as · function as
Notice (Activity 1): find the main verb, then the reduced clause.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite with is used as, a cleft sentence and a past participle.
Likely errors: *did not appear by · *regarded a second capital · *which established by.
Use (Activity 4): an idea ahead of its time.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: GEV-her ne-SI-be, KAY-se-ri, ma-KARR-ı u-le-MÂ, gı-yâ-sed-DIN key-hus-REV.
Stress: sys-tem-AT-ic, the-o-RET-i-cal, CLIN-i-cal, civ-i-li-ZA-tion.
beforeReading: Ask: “Do doctors learn better in a classroom, at a patient’s bedside or both? Why?”
duringReading: First reading: What is the main claim of the chapter?
Second reading: put three dates on a time line.
Underline every past participle that follows a noun.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Time line; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: an idea ahead of its time; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What evidence does the chapter give for its main claim?
Why might Kayseri have been called the center of scholars?
Why do you think the complex became a museum of civilization?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Kayseri” and “Makarr-ı Ulemâ” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: surviving, regarded as, functions as.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the time line with the centuries written in, and highlight the main verbs.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a four-sentence museum label using two reduced relative clauses.

formativeAssessment: Explains the main claim with evidence.
Uses not … until and a reduced relative clause correctly.
expectedResponses: The Gevher Nesibe Complex is the oldest surviving Anatolian Seljuk hospital and the first hospital and medical school built as one complex. Its bedside training appeared in the 13th century, while Europe did not develop this kind of training until the 16th and 17th centuries.
content.transferTask: Write about an invention or idea that was ahead of its time.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners find the main verb in the long sentences?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “It was not until … that …” and one with a reduced relative clause.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains why the complex was ahead of its time.
Compares dates accurately.
Uses not … until and a reduced relative clause.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
columns: Hospital and school as one complex
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners give a one-minute overview of why the Gevher Nesibe Complex was ahead of its time. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A summarizes paragraph 1 and B summarizes paragraphs 2 and 3. Each partner asks a follow-up question about the other’s part.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence about Europe. Asker asks “How many centuries earlier was Anatolia?” Explainer calculates and explains.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A foreign doctor visiting Kayseri asks why this museum matters for the history of medicine. The learner answers in one minute.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “The building complex, which today functions as the Museum of the Seljuk Civilization, was constructed by the Anatolian Seljuk ruler Gıyâseddin Keyhusrev I in honor of his sister, Gevher Nesibe Sultan.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what the Gevher Nesibe Complex is and why it was ahead of its time. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “What kind of evidence does the writer use to show the complex was ahead of its time?” (Comparisons with Europe and with the later Ottoman medical school.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give both “firsts” and support the claim with one comparison.

thinkAloud.strategy: Find the core of a long sentence
thinkAloud.sentence: The systematic medical training established in Anatolia in the 13th century, which combined theoretical education with clinical training at the bedside, did not appear in Europe until the 16th and 17th centuries.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: The subject is long, so I look for the verb: “did not appear”. The “which” clause tells me what kind of training it was. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “At the time the Gevher Nesibe Complex was established, Konya served as the capital of the Seljuk Sultanate, while Kayseri was regarded as a second capital and was known as ‘Makarr-ı Ulemâ’ (the center of scholars).”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What was Kayseri known as?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences about a place in your country that was ahead of its time.
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question.

content.chapter: Chapter 2: A Princess and a Commander
objectives: Retell the legend as a chain of causes and results.
Recognize how the text signals a legend.
Explain the roles of the people in the story.
Use participle clauses, due to, -ing clauses of result and purpose infinitives.
content.pedagogy: A human story that the text frames as a legend (“According to legend”). It is narrated with dense B2 linking: participle openings, “due to” + noun phrase and an -ing result clause. A cause-result chain lets learners retell it calmly and accurately.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The text presents the love story as a legend.
Gevher Nesibe was the Sultan’s younger sister, not his daughter.
“Contract” here means “catch an illness”, not “a written agreement”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: following + noun phrase · due to + noun phrase · comma + -ing clause of result · to + verb (purpose) · oppose / be against
Notice (Activity 1): causing her to contract … expresses a result.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then switch between noun phrases and clauses.
Likely errors: *Due to there was no … · *Followed the martyrdom · *causing her contract.
Use (Activity 4): retell a legend.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: kı-lıç-ars-LAN the SEC-ond, sü-va-Rİ a-la-YI.
Stress: CAV-al-ry, MAR-tyr-dom, tu-ber-cu-LO-sis, fa-CIL-i-ty.
Note: con-TRACT (verb) and CON-tract (noun).
beforeReading: Ask: “What is the difference between a legend and a historical fact?”
duringReading: First reading: Who are the people in the story?
Second reading: make a cause-result chain.
Find the phrase that shows this is a legend.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Legend or fact?; 5–12 First reading; 12–19 Cause-result chain; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: retell a legend; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the Sultan send the commander away?
How does the text link her grief and her illness?
Why is the lack of a medical facility important for the rest of the book?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “According to Legend” and “Kılıçarslan II” when the picture is in place.
Read the sad parts calmly and briefly. The focus of the next chapter is the good that came from them.
Word Notes: courtier, grief, contract, Due to, proper, apologized to, commander.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chain with the first and last boxes filled.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Retell the legend in five sentences using following, due to and an -ing result clause.

formativeAssessment: Explains how one event caused another.
Uses due to and following with noun phrases.
expectedResponses: According to legend, Gevher Nesibe loved a commander, but her brother opposed the relationship and sent the commander to war. Following his martyrdom, her grief weakened her, causing her to contract tuberculosis, and due to the lack of a proper hospital she died young.
content.transferTask: Retell a legend you know as a chain of causes and results.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep the legend separate from historical facts?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “Due to …” and one ending with “…, causing …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Retells the events in order.
Links causes and results.
Uses due to and following correctly.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners retell the legend of Gevher Nesibe Sultan and explain the cause-and-effect chain. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner explains the chain from grief to death to a partner. The partner restates it with “which led to”.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence with “Following”. Asker asks “What caused her illness?” Explainer explains “contract tuberculosis”.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A museum guide tells a school group the legend in one minute, reminding them that it is a legend.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “When she was on her deathbed, Gıyâseddin Keyhusrev I apologized to her and asked for her final wish.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, the legend of Gevher Nesibe Sultan. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the writer say ‘According to legend’?” (The love story is told by tradition and is not certain history.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners link at least three causes and effects and mark the story as a legend.

thinkAloud.sentence: Following the commander’s martyrdom, Gevher Nesibe Sultan’s intense grief weakened her, eventually causing her to contract tuberculosis.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Following” gives the first event. “Weakened her” is the next step, and “eventually causing” gives the final effect. I can write it as three steps. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “However, her elder brother, Sultan Gıyâseddin Keyhusrev I, opposed the relationship and did not allow them to marry.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: Why did the Sultan send the commander to war?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences: What can a legend teach even if we are not sure it really happened?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question.

content.chapter: Chapter 3: The Last Wish
objectives: Explain the aims of Gevher Nesibe’s last wish.
Identify the formal, solemn tone of her words.
Report her wish in indirect speech.
Use Let + object + base verb, negative prefixes and the present perfect of can.
content.pedagogy: A short first-person text that turns grief into a plan for others: the basis of a charitable foundation (vakıf). Its formal register (“no hope of recovery”, “renowned physicians”, “stand as a charity”) is worth noticing and comparing with everyday language.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The text says “As the legend goes”; her words belong to the legend.
She did not ask doctors to work without pay; she asked that patients pay nothing.
“Cause” here means “an aim people support”, not “a reason”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: Let + object + base verb / be + past participle · present perfect of can (has been able to) · negative prefixes in- / un- with -able · reported requests (ask … to; insist that … should)
Notice (Activity 1): incurable, untreatable.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then report her wish.
Likely errors: *Let surgeons trained · *Let no one to pay · *asked him use.
Use (Activity 4): a cause worth supporting.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: in-CUR-a-ble, un-TREAT-a-ble, re-NOWNED, phy-SI-cian, re-COV-er-y.
Intonation: read her words slowly and solemnly; pause after each “Let …”.
beforeReading: Ask: “If you could leave one thing to help people after you, what would it be?”
duringReading: First reading: What did she ask for?
Second reading: complete the two-part chart.
Underline the formal words and find everyday equivalents.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–18 Two-part chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a cause worth supporting; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did she want the hospital to be free?
Why did she ask for physicians to be trained there as well?
How does this chapter change the mood of the story?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Last Wish” and “A Charity” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: incurable, recovery, untreatable, charity, entire fortune, cause.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with one item in each column.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Rewrite her wish as a short modern charity statement of four sentences.

formativeAssessment: Explains the aims of the wish.
expectedResponses: In her last wish, Gevher Nesibe asked her brother to use her wealth to establish a free hospital that would heal the sick, search for cures and train physicians. She then donated her entire fortune to this cause.
content.transferTask: Write about a cause you would support and what it should do.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see how a personal loss became a public good?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “Let … ” and one reported request with “asked … to”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the aims of the wish.
Notices formal language.
Uses Let and a reported request.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners summarize the four requests in Gevher Nesibe’s last wish. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A explains the first half of the wish and B explains the second half. Each partner identifies the most important request.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the wish. Asker asks “What does ‘a single dirham’ show?” Explainer explains the emphasis.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A charity worker explains to donors why free health care matters, using Gevher Nesibe’s wish as an example.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “She then donated her entire fortune to this cause.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what Gevher Nesibe asked for in her last wish. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “What does the repeated ‘Let …’ do in the wish?” (It turns her wishes into clear instructions.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give four requests and explain the function of “Let”.

thinkAloud.sentence: Let no one pay a single dirham (penny).
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “A single” makes the sentence stronger. She does not only want low prices; she wants everything to be free. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Let this hospital heal the sick, while also searching for cures to untreatable diseases.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What did she do with her fortune?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences: Why is a charity in someone’s name a good way to remember them?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with an example.

content.chapter: Chapter 4: The Twin Madrasas
objectives: Describe how the madrasa and the hospital were built.
Explain why they are called the Twin Madrasas.
Explain how historians know the construction date.
Use purpose infinitives, past passives and be known as.
content.pedagogy: A short factual chapter that moves from legend to evidence: the inscription on the gate gives the date. It is a good moment to discuss how historians use inscriptions as primary sources.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The madrasa and the hospital are two buildings, not one.
The date comes from the inscription, not from the legend.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: to + verb (purpose) / in order to · past passive (was completed, was buried) · be known as · it took + time + to
Notice (Activity 1): To fulfill his sister’s will …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite with because, in order to and it took.
Likely errors: *For fulfill · *Construction completed in two years (meaning) · *known like.
Use (Activity 4): how a place got its name.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: gı-yâ-Sİ-ye, şi-fâ-İ-ye, dâ-rüş-şi-FÂ.
Stress: MAD-ra-sa, in-SCRIP-tion, con-STRUC-tion, ful-FILL.
beforeReading: Ask: “How do we know when an old building was built?”
duringReading: First reading: What was built, and why?
Second reading: find the date and its source.
Find why people call them twins.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–10 First reading; 10–16 Date and source; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: how a place got its name; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the Sultan build the madrasa and the hospital?
Why is the inscription important evidence?
Why do you think she was buried inside the madrasa?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Twin Madrasas” and “The Inscription” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: tomb.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a frame: “To …, he built … It was completed … They are known as … because …”.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short guide text for visitors standing at the main gate.

formativeAssessment: Describes what was built and why.
Names the source of the date.
expectedResponses: To fulfill his sister’s will, Gıyâseddin Keyhusrev built a madrasa and a hospital, which are known as the Twin Madrasas because they stand side by side. The inscription on the gate gives the date 1205–1206.
content.transferTask: Write about a place and how it got its name.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners understand the difference between legend and inscription?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “To + verb, …” and one with “be known as”.

rubricLevels.secure: Describes the buildings and their purpose.
Names the inscription as the source.
Uses a passive and be known as.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain how the Twin Madrasas were built and how we know their date. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: One learner explains the chapter to a partner. The partner restates why the buildings are called twins.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the last sentence. Asker asks “Where does the date come from?” Explainer explains “inscription”.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A tourist asks what the inscriptions on old buildings tell us. The learner answers using this chapter.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Gevher Nesibe Sultan was buried in her tomb inside the madrasa.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what the Sultan built to fulfill his sister’s will. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why is an inscription good evidence for a date?” (It was written when the building was made.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners name both buildings and explain “to fulfill his sister’s will”.

thinkAloud.sentence: To fulfill his sister’s will, Gıyâseddin Keyhusrev built a madrasa (Gıyâsiye Medresesi), and then a hospital (Şifâiye).
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “To fulfill” gives the purpose. The brackets give the names of the two buildings. “And then” shows the order. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Construction of the hospital was completed in two years.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What date is on the inscription?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences about an inscription or plaque you have seen.
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: Learning Beside the Patients
objectives: Describe how teaching and treatment were organized.
Separate facts from uncertain claims.
Explain the heating system and the use of the courtyards.
Use hedging language: suggest, likely, although this is not certain, be believed to have + past participle.
content.pedagogy: An important chapter for academic reading: the writer carefully marks what is certain and what is only probable. Learners practice reading the writer’s stance, which is central to B2 reading and to honest writing about history.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The text does not say for certain that students lived in the complex; it says “likely”.
The staff list is “generally believed”, not proven.
Outpatients were examined in the courtyards, not admitted.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: evidence + suggest that · likely (adverb) · although this is not certain · be believed to have + past participle · It is believed that …
Notice (Activity 1): is generally believed to have included.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite with impersonal reporting.
Likely errors: *Excavations are suggested · *is believed to included · *It believes that.
Use (Activity 4): what the evidence suggests.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: ex-ca-VA-tions, IN-tern-ists, PHAR-ma-cist, OUT-pa-tients.
Weak form: “to have” /tə hæv/ → /tə(h)əv/ in fast speech.
beforeReading: Ask: “How can a historian know how an old hospital worked?”
duringReading: First reading: How was education organized?
Second reading: mark facts F and careful guesses G.
Underline every word that shows uncertainty.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–18 Facts and guesses; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: what the evidence suggests; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the writer use words like likely and suggest?
What does the heating system tell us about the builders?
Why compare the staff with the Keykâvus Dârüşşifâ in Sivas?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Theory and Practice” and “Heating” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: Excavations, internists, surgeons.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a two-column chart with the uncertainty words already highlighted.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Rewrite two hedged sentences as if they were certain, then explain why that would be dishonest.

formativeAssessment: Explains how teaching and treatment were organized.
expectedResponses: Students learned theory at the Gıyâsiye and practiced at the Şifâiye. Excavations suggest that the buildings were heated from below, and students likely lived in small rooms, while the staff is only believed to have included physicians, surgeons and a pharmacist.
content.transferTask: Write about a place, mixing facts and careful guesses.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners notice the difference between fact and guess?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “Evidence suggests that …” and one with “… is believed to have …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Separates certain and uncertain information.
Explains how the complex worked.
Uses suggest, likely or believed to have.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners describe how the institution worked, separating facts from likely ideas. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A explains up to “outpatients” and B explains the rest. Each partner sorts one statement into “certain” or “likely”.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence about the staff. Asker asks “Is this certain?” Explainer finds the words that show uncertainty.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A modern medical student asks how training 800 years ago compares with today. The learner answers.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “In the 13th century, education at this medical institution combined theory at the Gıyâsiye and practical training at the Şifâiye.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how students learned and how the institution was staffed. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Which words in this chapter show uncertainty?” (Suggest, likely, although this is not certain, generally believed.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners report the staff with hedging and name the two buildings’ roles.

thinkAloud.sentence: Although this is not certain, the staff is generally believed to have included a chief physician with his assistants, at least two internists, two surgeons, and a pharmacist.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Although this is not certain” and “is generally believed” show the writer is careful. I report it as a likely picture, not a fact. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Excavations suggest that the buildings were heated from below using steam from a nearby bathhouse.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What were the courtyards used for in summer?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences: Why must historians be careful with words like “certain” and “likely”?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one example.

content.chapter: Chapter 6: Great Teachers and Books
objectives: Describe the scholars who taught at the complex.
List the subjects taught at the Gıyâsiye.
Explain where the medical knowledge came from.
Use non-defining relative clauses, appositives, among them, including and on the other hand.
content.pedagogy: A dense chapter full of names. The key reading skill is to separate the main clause from the extra information added in commas and brackets. The chapter also shows how knowledge travelled from Greek and Roman sources through Arabic translations to Anatolia.
priorKnowledge: Relative clauses with who and which.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Hippocrates and Galen were not teachers there; their works were taught in Arabic translation.
Theory was taught at the Gıyâsiye; clinical training took place at the Şifâiye.
“Commentary” here is a book that explains another book, not a sports commentary.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: non-defining relative clauses · appositives (nicknamed …; Mevlânâ’s close friend …) · among them · including · particularly · on the other hand
Notice (Activity 1): extra information in commas.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then combine sentences.
Likely errors: *Between them · *included the works (as linker) · *who he died.
Use (Activity 4): a teacher who shaped others.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: ab-dül-la-TÎF, kut-büd-DİN eş-şî-RÂ-zî, sad-red-DİN ko-ne-VÎ, i-na-yet-ul-LAH, keh-HÂL.
Stress: oph-thal-MOL-o-gist, phys-i-OL-o-gy, a-NAT-o-my, COM-men-tar-y.
beforeReading: Ask: “Which books or teachers from other cultures have shaped what you learn at school?”
duringReading: First reading: Who taught there?
Second reading: complete a chart: name, description, field.
Bracket every phrase that adds extra information.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–19 Scholars chart; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a teacher who shaped others; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did students study philosophy and languages as well as medicine?
What does the teaching of Hippocrates and Galen in Arabic show?
Why do you think great scholars came to Kayseri?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Ekmeleddin al-Nahcuvânî” and “Hippocrates and Galen” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: commentary, lectured on, Clinical.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with names already written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short profile of one scholar using an appositive and a relative clause.

formativeAssessment: Explains where the knowledge came from.
Uses a non-defining relative clause correctly.
expectedResponses: Famous scholars such as Abdüllatîf al-Baghdadî and Kutbüddin al-Shirazi taught at the Gıyâsiye. They lectured on philosophy, religious sciences, languages, anatomy and physiology, and taught the works of al-Razi and Ibn Sînâ, as well as Arabic translations of Hippocrates and Galen.
content.transferTask: Write about a scholar or teacher you admire.
content.teacherReflection: Could learners find the main clause in the long sentences?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with a non-defining relative clause and one with “including”.

rubricLevels.secure: Describes the scholars and subjects.
Explains where the knowledge came from.
Uses a relative clause or appositive.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners present the teachers and curriculum of the Gıyâsiye. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner explains to a partner what “a commentary on Ibn Sînâ’s al-Qanun fi’l-Tibb” means. The partner explains why such a book is useful.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the list of subjects. Asker asks “Which are medical and which are not?” Explainer sorts them.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A librarian asks which classic texts were taught there. The learner answers and names their authors.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Clinical training, on the other hand, took place at patients’ bedsides in the Şifâiye Hospital.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?

metadata.title: The Gevher Nesibe Hospital B2 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: The Gevher Nesibe Hospital and Medical School (Gevher Nesibe Dârüşşifâsı ve Tıp Medresesi)
metadata.estimatedDuration: 11 chapter units of 45 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow extended texts about history, buildings and science, and who can produce clear, detailed explanations and evaluations.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B2 reading, listening, speaking and writing through the history of the Gevher Nesibe Dârüşşifâ in Kayseri: the legend, the buildings, medical education and music therapy, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does, then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world. At B2, learners also notice how the writer signals certainty (suggest, likely, is believed to have, none are known to have) and keeps legend, evidence and conclusion apart, and they use these forms in their own writing.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 11 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Notice → Build → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a picture, a date or a plan of the building.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: legend, cause chain, evidence and conclusion, attributed view or evaluation.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B2 transfer: an explanation, evaluation or argument about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context, a picture or a plan before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus production, exit tickets and the cumulative review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us? How certain is the writer?), let learners formulate the rule, then confirm it and practice it in context. B2 targets include reduced and non-defining relative clauses, participle clauses, cleft sentences, hedging, impersonal reporting and passive modals. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: reduced relative clauses (established by …) · not … until / It was not until … that · while (contrast) · be regarded as · function as
Ch2: following + noun phrase · due to + noun phrase · comma + -ing clause of result · to + verb (purpose) · oppose / be against
Ch3: Let + object + base verb / be + past participle · present perfect of can (has been able to) · negative prefixes in- / un- with -able · reported requests (ask … to; insist that … should)
Ch4: to + verb (purpose) / in order to · past passive (was completed, was buried) · be known as · it took + time + to
Ch5: evidence + suggest that · likely (adverb) · although this is not certain · be believed to have + past participle · It is believed that …

Ch7: sentential which (…, which suggests that …) · make it + adjective + to · present and past passives · It is believed that … / … is believed to have been …

Ch9: defining relative clauses (students who …) · be based on · consist of / be made up of · according to · reporting verbs (indicate that) · continue to + verb
Ch10: by + -ing (method, parallel forms) · should be + past participle · based on · at specific times · reporting verbs (state, note, examine, classify, explain) · it is clear that

languageFocus: Every one of the 11 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Notice → Build → Use (4 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.

metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the reasoning target: one paragraph at a time, charts given in part, selected vocabulary, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside details or opinions.

Chapters 2 and 3 are presented as a legend (“According to a famous story”, “As the legend goes”). Read them calmly; the death of the commander and of Gevher Nesibe are told briefly and should not be dramatized.
Treat mental health respectfully; never use the topic for jokes.
Bracketed Turkish names in the text belong to the teacher-approved story; they are read as they are.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The Gevher Nesibe Hospital links a Seljuk city with questions every community faces: how to care for the sick, how to train good doctors and how to turn a loss into a gift for others.

themes.title: Health care for everyone:
themes.description: Gevher Nesibe wanted a free hospital (Chapter 3). Discuss how communities today help people who cannot pay for care.

themes.title: Learning by doing:
themes.description: Students learned theory at the Gıyâsiye and practiced at the Şifâiye under masters (Chapters 5 and 9). Compare this with internships and clinical training today.

themes.title: Mind and body:
themes.description: The Dârüşşifâ had a psychiatric section with sound corridors for music and suggestion therapy (Chapters 8 and 10). Discuss why mental health matters.

themes.title: Knowledge from many cultures:
themes.description: Scholars taught al-Razi and Ibn Sînâ as well as Arabic translations of Hippocrates and Galen (Chapter 6). Discuss how knowledge travels between cultures.

actions: Find one health or charity organization in your area and write two sentences about what it does.
Make a short poster: “Five ways to look after your mind”.
Interview a nurse, doctor or pharmacist about how they learned their job.

metadata.title: The Gevher Nesibe Hospital B2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 30 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B2 learners who study the history of the Gevher Nesibe Dârüşşifâ alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Understand the 11 chapters of The Gevher Nesibe Hospital.
Find evidence in the text before answering.
Follow the legend, the buildings and the medical education of the Gevher Nesibe Dârüşşifâ.
Separate legend, facts and careful beliefs, and evaluate the legacy of the Dârüşşifâ with evidence.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 11.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One detail about the Gevher Nesibe Dârüşşifâ that surprised me, and why:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 11 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 30 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 4 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows compassion, responsibility, diligence and respect. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Compassion: Compassion: Gevher Nesibe wanted a free hospital, and the Dârüşşifâ cared for mental health with music and suggestion therapy (Chapters 3 and 8).
Responsibility: Responsibility: The Sultan fulfilled his sister’s will and built the madrasa and the hospital (Chapter 4).
Diligence: Diligence: Students studied many sciences and trained at patients’ bedsides under masters (Chapters 5 and 9).
Respect: Respect: The icâzet honored a chain of teachers, and scholars studied Greek, Roman and Islamic sources (Chapters 6 and 9).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 11, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Tell the story of Gevher Nesibe and her Dârüşşifâ in six sentences to someone at home, in your home language or in English.
